title: "Forecasting and Explaining U.S. Unemployment"
subtitle: "A machine-learning early-warning system using macroeconomic indicators"
toc: true

## Project Summary

This project examines whether publicly available macroeconomic indicators can
provide early-warning signals of future U.S. labor-market deterioration. It
forecasts unemployment 3, 6, and 12 months ahead using data from 1956 through
2025.

[View the GitHub Repository](https://github.com/manishkallu01-wq/DATA510-Session-2){.btn .btn-primary role="button"}

## Research Question

Which publicly available macroeconomic indicators provide the strongest
early-warning signals of future U.S. labor-market deterioration, and how
accurately can unemployment be forecast 3, 6, and 12 months in advance?

## Motivation

Early identification of labor-market deterioration can support policymakers,
businesses, investors, economists, and workforce agencies in making better
planning and resource-allocation decisions.

## Data

The analysis combines six public economic series:

| Indicator | Source | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Unemployment Rate | U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics | Forecast target |
| Consumer Price Index | U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics | Inflation |
| Federal Funds Rate | Federal Reserve | Monetary policy |
| Gross Domestic Product | U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis | Economic growth |
| Consumer Sentiment | University of Michigan | Consumer confidence |
| Recession Indicator | National Bureau of Economic Research | Economic-cycle conditions |

The final dataset contains 838 monthly observations covering 1956–2025.

## Data Pipeline

1. Download the six public datasets.
2. Clean and standardize date and value fields.
3. Convert quarterly GDP observations to monthly frequency.
4. Align and merge all series by month.
5. Create lag, momentum, inflation, growth, and economic-stress features.
6. Build model-ready datasets for each forecast horizon.

## Method

The project uses a time-based train-and-test split to avoid using future
information during model training.

Three models were compared:

- Linear Regression
- Random Forest
- Gradient Boosting

Forecast horizons:

- 3 months
- 6 months
- 12 months

Performance was evaluated using:

- Mean Absolute Error
- Root Mean Squared Error
- R²

## Results

The 3-month forecast produced the strongest performance, with an MAE of
approximately 0.42 unemployment percentage points and an R² of approximately
0.51.

Performance weakened at the 6-month and 12-month horizons, showing that
macroeconomic indicators are more useful for near-term early warning than for
precise long-term unemployment forecasting.

Important predictive factors included consumer sentiment, inflation, interest
rates, GDP growth patterns, and recession periods.

## Conclusion

Public macroeconomic indicators can provide meaningful near-term signals of
future unemployment conditions. The system is most useful as an early-warning
tool rather than as a precise long-range predictor.

## Limitations and Future Work

The analysis is limited to six national indicators and U.S. data through 2025.
Future work could incorporate state-level and industry-level labor data,
alternative forecast horizons, additional indicators, and advanced time-series
models.
